title: Watching a Run: The Robot as a Moving Picture, an Animated SVG Made From the Scenario and the Log, Opened in Any Browser

questions.question: Why draw a run as an SVG?
options: It is the smallest format there is
It is the only format with animation
It is text that any browser opens and animates, with no library
It needs a viewer to be installed
questions.explanation: The file is plain text with the numbers still in it, it opens in a browser, and it can be compared with diff.

questions.question: A 10 s run of 500 poses came to how much SVG?
options: 500 bytes
questions.explanation: About fifty bytes a pose, and some fifty times smaller than a video of the same run.

questions.question: At four times the speed the animation lasted:
options: 9.98 s, unchanged
questions.explanation: The run's 9.98 s divided by four.

questions.question: What must a robot picture do about the y axis?
options: Flip it, because SVG's points down and the robot's up
Nothing: the two agree
Swap it with x
Scale it by the picture's height
questions.explanation: Drawn without the flip, a left turn on the field is a right turn on the screen, and nothing looks wrong until it is compared with the robot.

questions.question: Why are the key times taken from the log's time stamps?
options: Time stamps are smaller than indices
The browser needs them in seconds
So that every run lasts the same
So a log with a gap plays with a gap
questions.explanation: Spacing the frames by index would close up a gap in the log. Using the stamps keeps the pause where it happened.

questions.question: Why must the bounds include the poses?
options: So the picture is always square
Because walls may be missing
To leave room for a legend
A robot that leaves the room is the run that most needs to be seen
questions.explanation: A view sized to the walls shows nothing of a robot that drove out through them.
